items.title: 4.1 Work done by a constant force

source_refs.note: Topic 4.1 with the chapter's opening lines and Figs. 4.1 to 4.4 (PDF 75-76, printed 72-73). The learning objectives are not reproduced; the running header reads 'Work, Energy and Force'.

blocks.text: Work is often thought of in terms of physical or mental effort. In physics, however, the term work involves two things: (i) force and (ii) displacement. We begin with the simple situation in which work is done by a constant force.

blocks.title: Work by a constant force
blocks.text: Consider an object pulled by a constant force F which displaces it through a displacement d in the direction of the force. Work W is defined as the product of the magnitude of the force F and the magnitude of the displacement d: W = F d ... (4.1).
Equation 4.1 shows that if the displacement is zero, no work is done even if a large force is applied: pushing on a wall may tire your muscles, but the work done is zero (Fig. 4.1).

blocks.alt: A boy leans forward and pushes a tall wall with both hands. An arrow labelled Force points towards the wall at its top; the wall is labelled Wall.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.1: A boy pushing a wall (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.1).

blocks.text: The force applied on a body may not always be in the direction of the displacement (Fig. 4.2).

blocks.alt: A boy pulls a block with a rope. The block is shown at its starting position A and again at B to the right. From the block, the force arrow F runs along the rope at an angle theta above the horizontal displacement arrow d.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.2: A force F at an angle theta to the displacement d of a block pulled from A to B (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.2).

blocks.text: If the force F makes an angle theta with the displacement d, the work done equals the product of the component of the force along the direction of the displacement and the magnitude of the displacement: W = (F cos theta) d = F d cos theta ... (4.2), or W = F . d ... (4.3) (Fig. 4.3).

blocks.alt: Axes with F upward and d to the right. A vector F starts at the origin at an angle theta above the d-axis. A dashed line drops from its tip to the d-axis, and the arrow along the d-axis from the origin to that point is labelled F cos theta.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.3: The component F cos theta of the force F along the displacement d (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.3).

blocks.text: Equation 4.3 shows that work is a scalar quantity. The unit of work is the joule (J); from Eq. 4.1, 1 J = 1 N m.

When a constant force acts through a distance d, the event can be plotted on a simple graph (Fig. 4.4), the distance along the x-axis and the force along the y-axis. As the force does not vary, the graph is a horizontal straight line. If the constant force F (newton) and the displacement d (metre) are in the same direction, the work done is F d (joule); the shaded area in Fig. 4.4 is also F d, so the area under a force-displacement curve can be taken to represent the work done by the constant force. If the force is not in the direction of the displacement, the graph is plotted between F cos theta and d.

blocks.alt: A graph with Force on the y-axis and distance on the x-axis. A shaded rectangle OPQR: O at the origin, P on the y-axis, Q above R, R on the x-axis. A double arrow F beside QR gives its height and a double arrow d below gives OR.
blocks.caption: Figure 4.4: Force-distance graph of a constant force: the rectangle OPQR (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 4.4).

items: If theta is less than 90 degrees, work is done and it is said to be positive work.
If theta = 90 degrees, no work is done.
If theta is greater than 90 degrees, the work done is said to be negative.
The SI unit of work is N m, known as the joule (J).
